newsitem.title: UK: UK earnings data may ease rate rise pressure.
newsitem.headline: UK earnings data may ease rate rise pressure.

text.p: Slower-than-expected growth in British average earnings in March may help to ease pressure for an early interest rate increase, but worries persist that rapidly falling unemployment may in time push pay settlements higher.
Economists welcomed official figures showing underlying average earnings rising 4.5 percent in the year to March and a downward revision in the February numbers to 4.5 percent from 5.0 percent.
But the 59,400 drop in April unemployment, giving a jobless rate of 5.9 percent, provided further evidence that the labour market was tightening.

"This will raise concern that the labour market is becoming progressively tighter and that skill shortages will ultimately feed through to higher earnings," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
However, Coleman believes such fears appear unjustified for the moment.
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International Europe, says pay settlements appear reasonably subdued at present but it is not clear whether or not average earnings have peaked.
"The key issue for average earnings is whether the continued fall in unemployment generates a more fundamental rise in average earnings. The outlook for that is not clear," he said.
"But with the speed of the fall in unemployment that we have seen, there is a threat that at some stage we will see settlements go up."
While financial markets had expected an average earnings figure of around 5.0 percent, economists noted that 4.5 percent is still uncomfortably high as far as the Bank of England is concerned.

The central bank's chief economist Mervyn King said on Tuesday that earnings growth much above 4.5 percent would be a worry and warned that the country was "sailing pretty close to the wind" on this front.
However, Dharshini David, an economist at HSBC Markets, said Wednesday's data confirmed that pay settlements still showed no signs of accelerating.
"As long as settlements remain moderate, earnings growth could fall further in the second half of the year, once the bonus round is fully out of the way," she said.
"With earnings growth now below the level seen at the end of last year, these figures are likely to ease the pressure for a further hike in base rates."
Simon Briscoe, an economist at Nikko Europe Plc, agreed.
"The inflation outlook has been materially changed by these numbers," he said. "The outlook for pay pressures is much less threatening than even these -- lower -- average earnings figures suggest."
Briscoe said the rise in earnings had been driven by bonuses and productivity increases and there was very little inflationary pressure in the broader economy.

Economists said the larger than expected drop in April unemployment still reflected distortions as a result of the Jobseekers' Allowance, which had led to many people who had previously claimed unemployment benefit coming off the register.

The new Labour government announced a review of the way labour market data are calculated, aimed at making them more credible. The present method measures people who meet strict requirements for claiming benefit rather than all those who would like work but are unable to find it.
Despite the distortions, many economists believe the figures still clearly point to a tightening labour market.
But Briscoe said the fall in claimant unemployment should be ignored.
"Job creation and other measures of unemployment (for which no new data have been released this month) show a less strong labour market," he said.
Shepperd of Yamaichi welcomed news that the data would be reviewed, although he said economists had become weary with repeated changes to the system.

"We have been living with manipulated, distorted data for 15 years," he said. "The problem has been the lack of a consistent historical series. One more change which establishes a sound basis for the figures would be welcome."
